description: We are a team from Torrey Pines High School.
summary: Launch Window is a 3D browser game in which platers develop and perform a space mission completely from start to finish. Players select destinations including the Moon, Mars, and even Titan, and players also select their scientific objective. Next, they are tasked with the development of the spacecraft with a set budget, with each custom part increasing or decreasing the overall cost. Prior to launch, there is an integration review in which players will analyze all aspects of the device including mass, total power, total energy change, and costs that allow users to detect issues early in the game. Once this is complete, players navigate the rocket from Earth all the way to the selected destination, battling the atmosphere, gravity, and other various challenges like solar flares. Once the destination is reached, players navigate through the complex landing process and after the mission receive feedback on how well they did the mission. Up to four users can play at the same time, and have roles including Mission Lead, Launch Engineer, Spacecraft Engineer or Science Lead.
details:
What it does and how it works:

At the beginning, a rocket is chosen from Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, Atlas V, SLS, or Saturn V. Custom designs could also be built from those base models. Then, a launch site and time of day is chosen. For the spacecraft, a user could change bus size from small to large, chemical or ion propulsion, and solar array size. There are also five mission requirements that turn green or red as they are met or not met. Then is the launch stage, where the rocket is launched like a conventional rocket into orbit. From there, the shuttle cruises to the destination while keeping watch for dangerous events like solar flares. At arrival, burn is held until a needle reaches the capture zone, with the planet's gravity a contributing factor to the amount of compensation needed. The score multiplies your science by spacecraft health, available power, data sent home, orbit choice and mission length, and is shown at the end of the mission.

Benefits:

Immediate feedback is provided for each decision made, helping students understand the cause and effect relationships via experimentation. Failed missions instantly show what went wrong, and what decision led to that failure. The game also keeps records of all performances, so students can understand what is good and what isn't.

Intended Impact:

I want students to understand why real missions are so difficult and take so long to design. Teachers can use to illustrate the depth and complexity of rocketry and space exploration to students in physics or engineering classes. Since the game runs solely on web, school Chromebooks can run it and it can be used in any classroom.

Tools:

I wrote this project in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. I used three.js for the graphics and Web Audio API for engine sound. The Earth uses NASA Blue Marble satellite imagery. Data comes from NSSDCA Planetary Fact Sheet, NASA MMRTG fact sheet, and JPL Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter figures. The code is hosted on GitHub. I used Claude to help with the programming and rocket graphics.

Creativity:

I tried to create a very unique design for my overall project, so I decided to have an assembly hall review before rollout. This feature helps students see their own creativity and unique rocket and spacecraft by breaking it down to smaller parts. The flying controls I settled on A and D, which are standard gaming controls.

Factors Considered:

I kept the physics as accurate as possible but simplified costs to make sure the mission can take just a few minutes. Prompts pop up each step, and autopilot can take over when a student worries about a crash. Graphics can also scale down on older computers to preserve frame rate. The game only uses public domain NASA data and no branding, and is released under Apache 2.0 license.
